name: Cynodon

project_scope.region: Hays County and Central Texas crew recognition
project_scope.native_status: Cynodon dactylon INTRODUCED in Texas per Kew; no native restoration planting endorsement
project_scope.cultivar_caution: Many common and hybrid turfgrass cultivars occur; exact C. dactylon x C. transvaalensis hybrid assignment is not reliable from a mowed sterile turf photograph.

look_here_first: Only ONE Cynodon species is installed here: introduced Bermudagrass, C. dactylon. Start with its spreading fine turf mat and ABOVEGROUND slender runner; then inspect the collar shoulder HAIRS (image already has a correct built-in arrow) and the TINY ciliolate/HAIR-FRINGED MEMBRANOUS ligule with a hand lens. A live flowering culm shows several slender finger-like unilateral racemes from nearly ONE shared point (verified built-in arrows); the close-up distinguishes pale/pink feathery stigma from pendent orange anther (already arrowed). For definitive vegetative confirmation, uncover a SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOME with buds and a genuinely ROOTED surface node, neither of which is actually photographed here. Do not assume an unflowering turf cultivar is pure C. dactylon rather than Cynodon turf complex.
shared_genus_traits: Spreading perennial grasses (often turf) with stolons and in many taxa rhizomes.
Narrow mostly short blades and short collar ligule, often hairs.
One top cluster of 2–9 slender finger-like racemes with spikelets in rows on one side.
Actual small spikelets not whole 'seeds'; use macro to tell two tight rows apart.
Cultivated turf types may not flower; treat uncertain mowed hybrid mixes as Cynodon sp. or bermudagrass turf complex.

crew_lookalikes.what: Finger clusters can be slightly staggered, broader often hairy leaves, membranous ligule; annual no scaly perennial rhizomes.
Stiffer finger seedhead and flattened whitish clump crown, jagged membranous ligule, annual.
Multiple spaced whorls of spokes vertically up a stalk, like tiered windmill.
Usually pair of V-shaped seedhead branches, moist soils, membranous ligule.
Local native buffalograss can spread by stolons; sex-specific flowerheads differ; don't wrongly label native turf as introduced Bermuda.
Coarser bunchy texture and multiple racemes at different heights along stem, not near one point.
Overlap most vegetative features; specific hybrid identification needs known cultivar parentage or expert material.

study_steps: 1. First decide whether you have a creeping grass: identify an ABOVEGROUND wiry stem with attached narrow leaves. The photographed stem does not show a connected root-emitting node.

2. Compare the existing CC0 hair-tuft image: its printed arrow really identifies LONG COLLAR HAIRS. The tiny inner ligule is a short HAIR-FRINGED MEMBRANOUS rim, not an isolated ribbon or the entire shoulder tuft.
3. At flowering follow the 4–6 mostly co-originating terminal fingers in the CC0 head photo; its two built-in arrows already correctly mark a ray and common branch point.
4. Separate reproductive roles in CC0 spikelet macro: branched pink STIGMA receives pollen; orange-brown dangling ANTHER produces pollen. Both baked arrows match the actual photo.

5. If the runner, flowering fingers and collar fit, carefully check both a genuinely root-bearing STOLON NODE and an UNDERGROUND SCALY RHIZOME with connected nodes/buds. Neither has a proven teaching photograph yet.

6. Compare true look-alikes: Digitaria has staggered finger origins and membranous ligule; Eleusine often stiffer fingers and flattened pale base; Chloris multiple flowerhead whorls; native buffalograss has separate male/female flower heads and hairy ligule may overlap.
7. Mowed sterile turf or C. transvaalensis hybrids may be impossible to resolve from a single photo; use Cynodon sp. or turf complex when certainty is unjustified.

glossary.definition: Aboveground horizontal stem with nodes and new shoots/roots
Underground stem with nodes, buds and often scaly leaves; distinct from root
Appendage at inner collar between leaf blade and sheath, in bermuda a tiny hair fringe
Seedhead branches spreading from approximately one point like fingers
Tiny grass spikelets clustered mostly on a single side of each narrow head branch
Ear-shaped projection at blade/sheath, absent in bermudagrass

field_note: Most restoration patches are vegetative: a flowering head is helpful but not required if runners and collar structures are verified. If only one unrooted stem piece is available, mark provisional.

comparison_lesson.title: Bermudagrass vs similar low grasses in Hays parks
comparison_lesson.core_rule: A star-shaped head alone is not a species ID. Use 3 or more of: (1) actual ABOVEground runner and actual UNDERground scaly rhizome; (2) tiny fringed collar with long shoulder hairs; (3) typically 4–6 one-sided terminal fingers joined near one point; (4) live habitat and rooting-node/cultivar context.
comparison_lesson.photo_evidence: Six existing CC-licensed *C. dactylon* photo panels reused. Five photographic arrows are printed directly on three CC0 JPEGs, and one separate browser marker identifies only an aboveground stem/runner. Not one photo shows the actual underground rhizome or rooted node. No invented root arrows.

comparisons.clue: Low vigorous turf mat; wiry surface stolons plus often scaly rhizomes; short ciliolate membrane and long collar hairs; several fine one-sided terminal seedhead fingers
comparisons.photo_status: 6 exact-source photo-led panels, real collar/head/stigma/anther/runner anatomy labels

comparisons.clue: Crabgrass often annual with branching fingers slightly staggered up tip; clear membranous ligule, usually no durable scaly perennial rhizomes
comparisons.photo_status: Compare visually in Digitaria card; not an image of bermudagrass

comparisons.clue: Goosegrass often has hard stiff radiating fingers, low compressed silvery-white base and a membranous ligule
comparisons.photo_status: Look-alike, no borrowed photo from unrelated species

comparisons.clue: Multiple separated whorls of flowerhead spokes on a tallish stem rather than one group from the tip
Native buffalograss also makes creeping stolons and can have very short hairy ligule; its distinct male and female inflorescences separate it from Bermuda
comparisons.photo_status: NATIVE look-alike; important to avoid a false introduced-weed call

comparisons.clue: Nimblewill has creeping leafy stems and short membrane but NARROW contracted panicle instead of the separated terminal fan of fingers
Sterile mowed turf can share runner, collar and leaf characters; do not resolve specific species/hybrid without reproductive or origin data
comparisons.photo_status: Taxonomic hold, not a standalone source-certified species photo

comparison_lesson.cautions: Kew describes a ciliolate membrane 0.2–0.3 mm; FNA about 0.5 mm of hairs. These do not justify 'absolutely no membrane'. The photographed collar tuft is longer hairs at the blade/sheath shoulders, not a measured ligule. Digitate flowering clusters recur in many genera; native buffalograss sometimes also bears a hairy collar. Photo source determinations for hybrids are provisional.

visual_comparison.title: Bermudagrass — runner, hair fringe and fingered flowers
visual_comparison.subtitle: Six genuinely archived photos from the 8-image species media collection; five already baked-in arrows on three CC0 originals plus one conservative browser runner arrow. Exact original photo rights and introduced-Texas warning preserved.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BERMUDA: creeper with stolon + scaly rhizome; SHORT ciliolate membrane plus white collar tufts; radiating ONE-SIDED fingers. Shared seedhead shape alone proves nothing.

items.label: 1 · HABIT — fine dense spreading turf
items.image_role: Actual credited Texas lawn-mat image; multiple fine spreading blades, no individual rooted node visible
items.caption: Existing CC BY Sam Kieschnick source photo shows a low fine-leaved patch. This alone is NOT proof of C. dactylon, root type, cultivar, or a pure-species lawn; start the ID here and then find the real running stems.
items.why_it_matters: Crew learns the everyday lawn/gateway appearance, with an explicit warning that mown turf and other grasses overlap.
items.creator: (c) Sam Kieschnick, some rights reserved (CC BY)
items.photo_status: Existing physically verified CC BY field image, original JPEG manually re-inspected 2026-10-21, no arrow placed on untraceable mat roots.

items.label: 2 · ABOVEGROUND RUNNER — connected leafy stem
items.image_role: Existing CC0 Texas-source photograph of a wiry stem held by fingers with narrow lateral leaves and leafy stem shoots; no visibly rooted soil-level node
items.caption: An aboveground slender horizontal stem with attached narrow leaf blades is visibly held over fingers. This is a stolon/runner candidate; roots visibly growing from an attached node are NOT established here, and no underground rhizome is exposed.
items.why_it_matters: Crew can distinguish a visible surface runner from a leaf blade, but must follow the connected plant to soil for actually rooted nodes.
items.creator: no rights reserved
items.photo_status: Existing exact photo ID 410585094 CC0, archived JPEG physically pixel-inspected 2026-10-21, one browser marker for visible wiry runner only; no root-location arrow.

items.label: 3 · COLLAR — real pale hair tuft
items.image_role: Exact CC0 source image with already physically drawn 'Collar hair tuft' arrow onto correct pale hairs at blade–sheath junction
items.caption: The *existing image itself* already has a label and arrow correctly pointing to conspicuous whitish hairs at the grass collar/shoulder. Those hairs are visually real, but the tiny inner fringed membrane (ligule, often around 0.2–0.5 mm) is NOT separately measured from the photo.
items.why_it_matters: Hairy collar helps distinguish bermudagrass from crabgrass/goosegrass with more obvious membranous ligules, but collar hairs alone cannot prove species.
items.creator: no rights reserved
items.photo_status: CC0 exact source image 410585092, pre-existing embedded printed arrow VERIFIED against committed JPEG pixels 2026-10-21. Do NOT overlay a duplicate browser arrow or label the invisible membrane.

printed_image_arrows.label: Collar hair tuft
printed_image_arrows.anatomy: visible long white hairs on shoulder of blade-sheath junction

items.label: 4 · DIGITATE HEAD — thin fingers from almost one point
items.image_role: Exact CC0 original with pre-existing correct printed arrows to one fingerlike terminal raceme and common branch origin
items.caption: The previously annotated source JPEG visibly shows five narrow flowering fingers radiating at nearly the same point on the culm. Its baked-in labels correctly point to a fingerlike ray and the shared branch point; scattered spikelets line the branches. Fingered inflorescences are NOT unique to bermudagrass.
items.why_it_matters: Teach terminal branch origin first, then compare staggered Digitaria, stiffer Eleusine, and tiered Chloris.
items.creator: no rights reserved
items.photo_status: CC0 exact source image 410585068: two PRE-EXISTING embedded printed arrows ('Fingerlike ray' and 'Shared branch point') physically checked 2026-10-21. No duplicate browser markers.

printed_image_arrows.label: Shared branch point
printed_image_arrows.anatomy: several branches converge near one culm tip

items.label: 5 · REPRODUCTIVE MICRO — stigma is not anther
items.image_role: Existing CC0 annotated original of grass spikelets with visibly separate pink feathery stigmas and drooping orange-brown anthers
items.caption: The saved source JPEG contains two already-correct arrows: branched pink feathery STIGMA and elongated pendent orange-brown ANTHER. This shows real flower anatomy on a one-sided spikelet-bearing branch, not the underground rhizome or a mature seed.
items.why_it_matters: Teach crew the difference between pollen-producing anther and pollen-receiving stigma; do not mistake either for bristles or grass seed.
items.creator: no rights reserved
items.photo_status: CC0 exact photo 410585069: embedded printed 'Feathery stigma' and 'Hanging anther' arrows VERIFIED on actual committed JPEG, 2026-10-21. Browser markers intentionally none.

items.label: 6 · SECOND FULL HEAD — check the whole flowerhead
items.image_role: Existing credited Dan Johnson CC BY source photograph of short narrow fingered flowering head held on open palm, plus nearby unconnected grass vegetation
items.caption: A second full flowering head shows several slender radiating branches and a hand for rough scale. Fine spikelet arrangement can be followed along the fingers, but neither an exact branching threshold nor a species-specific rhizome is proven here.
items.why_it_matters: Seeing the star head in two real observations helps recognition without treating each photo as an independent species voucher.
items.creator: Dan Johnson
items.photo_status: Previously archived Dan Johnson CC BY original photo pixels visually examined 2026-10-21; source identity follows observation; no unsupported individual spikelet measurement arrow.
